Mammals. A class of endothermic vertebrates characterized by hair, mammary glands, and a single bone in the lower jaw called the dentary, uniquely positioned for jaw articulation. They evolved from therapsid synapsids during the Triassic period but remained small and marginal until the Cenozoic era. The extinction of dinosaurs allowed rapid diversification. Today, mammals inhabit every terrestrial ecosystem and the oceans, from the smallest insectivores to the largest whales.

Mammals possess three middle-ear bones called malleus, incus, and stapes—derived from reptilian jaw bones. This is an innovation that enhances hearing and marks a key evolutionary transition. Mammary glands secrete milk to nourish offspring, reducing parental burden and allowing mothers to provision young with precisely calibrated nutrition.

Hair provides insulation and thermoregulation, enabling mammals to maintain high body temperature and activity in cold climates where reptiles cannot survive. The diaphragm, a sheet of muscle beneath the lungs, enables efficient air exchange in mammals, supporting higher metabolic rates than reptiles require.

Monotremes—egg-laying mammals like the platypus—are considered the most primitive living mammals, retaining features lost in marsupials and placental mammals. Placental mammals achieve higher fetal development in utero, with gestation lasting months, giving newborns a competitive advantage over marsupial young.

The Cenozoic "Age of Mammals" saw rapid adaptive radiation. Primates, carnivores, ungulates, and cetaceans diversified within roughly 66 million years. Mammals are the only animals with a four-chambered heart and a muscular diaphragm—innovations allowing efficient circulation and respiration at high metabolic rates.

The mammalian jaw consists of a single bone, the dentary, articulating directly with the skull. This contrasts sharply with the multiple bones in reptile jaws. Over 5400 species of mammals exist today, ranging from insectivores weighing less than a gram to blue whales exceeding 100 tons. They fill nearly every terrestrial and marine ecological niche.

Internal temperature regulation enabled mammals to exploit nocturnal and polar habitats unavailable to cold-blooded reptiles.

The Cenozoic era is the geological era dominated by mammals after dinosaur extinction. The Triassic period is when the first mammal-like synapsids transitioned into true mammals. Evolution is the process driving mammalian diversification and adaptation to new ecological niches. Vertebrates are the larger animal class to which all mammals belong. Human evolution is the specific lineage tracing primates from earlier mammalian ancestors. The Quaternary period is the recent geological period shaped by mammalian megafauna and human emergence.
